Introduction

I opened this column months ago but kept putting off writing for it. Recently, encouraged by fellow Zhihu users, and by the launch of Zhihu’s creator center, which showed me that hundreds of thousands of people had read my Zhihu answers, I decided to give the column the attention it deserves. Besides histories of the various fields of acoustics (architectural acoustics, virtual acoustics, psychoacoustics, NVH and so on) and acoustics fundamentals, my initial plan is to cover in detail the techniques of acoustic virtual reality and auralization; the theory of the Microflown particle velocity sensor and its applications in research and industry (mainly automotive NVH); and other topics I’ve worked on and can write about, such as beamforming and microphone arrays. Suggestions, corrections and contributions from fellow acousticians are very welcome. Let’s learn and grow together!

That was from the first article in my Zhihu column, Tech You Can Hear: Acoustics. Six months on, the column has passed 3,000 upvotes and, with a big push from Zhihu’s follower-promotion feature, 11,000 followers. Compared with the big names on WeChat, that’s a lot more than a teeny-weeny bit behind. So I thought I’d try a WeChat Official Account too and see what a bigger platform is like. After all, each article takes a dozen or more hours of work, and I’d like more people to see them. The direction is much the same as the vision I set out six months ago: histories of acoustics, popular science, industrial applications, case studies, future prospects and so on.

Enough chatter. On to the good stuff.

Background

Acoustics is an interdisciplinary field. From its beginnings in music to its wide use today in electronics and electrical appliances, ocean science, buildings, the environment, cars, railways and aviation, medicine, seismology and voice interaction, it has grown from a branch of physics into a major discipline inseparable from everyday life. The ultimate purpose of acoustics research is to serve our sense of hearing, the ear, and that is what makes it so important. Yet it was precisely this close tie to people that kept acoustics from getting much attention while manufacturing was booming. Only when manufacturing hit a plateau were people, who initiate technology and manufacturing and are their ultimate beneficiaries, taken into account. With a human-centered approach, subjective perception and comfort have gradually gained recognition and market influence. That is why more people should get to know acoustics, a discipline both ancient and full of life.

Architectural acoustics, also called room acoustics (this article uses “architectural acoustics” throughout), is one of the most traditional branches of acoustics and remains an important research topic today. The first thing that comes to mind is concert hall design, perhaps one of the few products where acoustics is considered from the very start of the design process. Since most human activity takes place indoors, the field covers not only concert halls but also bedrooms at home, factories, cinemas, libraries, offices (open-plan offices, so fashionable now, have even bigger noise problems, so many of the people who champion open spaces are also thinking about personal acoustic environments), schools, bars, car cabins and more.

Chronologically, architectural acoustics can be divided into roughly five stages:

  1. Up to 1930: from physical acoustics to the beginnings of architectural acoustics

  2. 1930–1960: early scientific exploration

  3. 1960–1980: the age of parameters

  4. 1980–present: the computer age

  5. 1990–present: auralization

1. Antiquity to 1930: from physical acoustics to the beginnings of architectural acoustics

As a branch of physics, acoustics developed relatively late; its theoretical foundations only matured in the second half of the 19th century. Its two founding fathers were both German: Hermann von Helmholtz (yes, the great Helmholtz, after whom the most fundamental equation in acoustics is named), who in 1862 published Die Lehre von den Tonempfindungen als physiologische Grundlage für die Theorie der Musik (On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music), and John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh (yes, that Rayleigh), who published The Theory of Sound in 1877 [1].

Architectural acoustics proper began with W. C. Sabine, who is widely regarded as its founder. Around 1900, he introduced the concepts of reverberation time and sound absorption by materials, together with the corresponding empirical formula, and pioneered the scientific study of architectural acoustics. Boston’s Symphony Hall, which he designed, is considered one of the finest concert halls in the world.

Around the 1930s, Eyring and Norris put Sabine’s equation on a theoretical footing and proposed a more rigorous way of calculating reverberation time, which became known as the Eyring equation.

2. 1930–1960: early scientific exploration

Building on Sabine’s theory of reverberation, a series of German acousticians from the 1930s onward, among them Erwin Meyer, Lothar Cremer, Vilhelm Jordan and Walter Reichardt, gradually consolidated the theoretical and experimental foundations of architectural acoustics. They built anechoic chambers lined with absorbing wedges (1936) and founded early acoustics journals: Akustische Zeitschrift (1936; renamed Acustica in 1951) and Acta Acustica (the two merged in 1996 as Acta Acustica united with Acustica).

The room response was also introduced in this period, by L. Cremer (another German…), to study how adding absorbing material affects a room’s reverberation. From then on, room responses gradually found their way into architectural acoustics.

It’s worth mentioning that in this period (1959), Dah-You Maa (Ma Dayou), the father of Chinese acoustics, took part in the acoustic design of the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. His 1939 paper in The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America (JASA), “Distribution of Eigentones in a Rectangular Chamber at Low Frequency Range,” is regarded as a foundation of rigorous room acoustics [2]. In the 1960s and 1970s, he invented the microperforated panel and worked out its design and theory [3].

3. 1960–1980: the age of parameters

In this period, impulse responses and transfer functions came into wide use in architectural acoustics, with outstanding contributions from Schroeder and Kuttruff. The Schroeder frequency was also introduced at this time. Based on a room’s size and reverberation time, it marks the frequency above which room modes overlap so densely that they can no longer be told apart and the field behaves statistically [4].

From the 1970s, architectural acoustics entered its “parametric” era: clarity, early decay time (EDT), lateral energy fraction (LEF), interaural cross-correlation (IACC), strength (G), proposed by the American Leo Beranek as a measure of spatial perception, apparent source width (ASW) and more, each with its own formula. But after all these parameters had been proposed and studied, it turned out that moderate levels, reverberation time and clarity cannot by themselves guarantee good acoustics. This set the stage for bringing in human subjective evaluation and auralization later on.

4. 1980–present: the computer age

Thanks to computers, people no longer had to compute Fourier transforms by hand to analyze spectra, and could gradually do without bulky test equipment such as the B&K level recorder below. When I taught lab classes during my PhD, we still used this very instrument to measure reverberation time. It’s purely analog, an electromechanical converter: a pen attached to the output traces the room’s energy decay on a paper strip, and you measure the trace with a ruler to calculate the reverberation time. It may look hopelessly primitive now, but you can’t help admiring the mechanical beauty of those days, and the crude yet remarkably intuitive and clear understanding it gave you.

At last, acoustic requirements could be addressed at the very start of building design, and simulation software came onto the market; CATT, EASE and ODEON are still widely used room acoustics packages today. Their advantages are obvious: they can quickly compute all kinds of room acoustic parameters, and in recent years they have added auralization, allowing both objective analysis of physical parameters and subjective evaluation. Their limitations are just as obvious. Most are based on geometrical acoustics, which is accurate only above the Schroeder frequency mentioned earlier: it treats sound waves as particles that carry energy but no phase, ignoring the wave nature of sound at low frequencies. So, as computers grew more powerful, numerical acoustics, which focuses on low-frequency simulation, also took off: the finite and boundary element methods (FEM/BEM), the finite-difference time-domain method (FDTD) and, more recently, the pseudospectral time-domain (PSTD) and discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods. But these numerical methods still need more computing power before they are ready for large-scale commercial use.

Computer modeling has to account for the three elements of sound propagation: the source, the path and the receiver.

For the source, you need to consider:

  • How large is the source itself?

  • Is there more than one source? Where are they?

  • What is the source’s directivity?

For the path:

  • a 3D model of the room

  • complex surfaces

  • the surface impedance of materials

  • phenomena other than specular reflection, such as diffraction, and scattering coefficients (for geometrical acoustics; numerical methods compute the full sound field and need not treat each phenomenon separately)

For the receiver:

  • the receiver’s size, position and orientation

  • binaural effects

Because so many factors can bias simulation results, in the mid-1990s the acoustics community ran its first round robin to compare room acoustics simulations [7].

5. 1990–present: auralization

Now we’ve finally arrived in the modern era. Auralization has nothing to do with auras: the word is the auditory counterpart of visualization. To take the simplest example: when you built an acoustic model of a room on a computer, you used to be able only to look at the parameters it computed; now, with auralization, you can also listen to how the room sounds, just as in the real world. Auralization is often combined with virtual reality, carrying real-world acoustic environments into the virtual world and, together with visualization, making you feel you’re really there. Say you’re playing a game and someone in front of you in a room fires a gun: the sound had better come from the front, or the experience suffers. And that sound has to be generated by rigorous acoustic computation.

As I said earlier, sound propagation has three elements, so naturally, carrying sound into the virtual world means dealing with all three.

Take my own PhD project. I worked on the source part, mainly modeling moving sources: I modeled things that move in real life (mostly vehicles such as cars and trains) and put them into virtual reality. By simulating in VR the traffic noise that a proposed urban plan or road layout would bring, decision-makers and ordinary residents alike can take part and judge it, instead of just staring at a pile of cold numbers and spectra, and together they can create acoustic environments that residents are happy with. Auralization is truly human-centered: it ties acoustics closely to people and involves them as fully as possible.

The examples below give you a feel for what auralization actually does (wear headphones for the binaural effect). As you follow the virtual person’s footsteps to different places, facing in different directions, what you hear changes. For a given source, the room layout shapes the signal received at each position, and the difference between the signals at the two ears lets you localize the source; don’t forget, humans are creatures fitted with two acoustic sensors. This kind of 3D acoustic experience is a concert hall designer’s dream: it helps them design more precisely and thoughtfully, so that every listener in every corner gets the best possible experience.

The concept of auralization dates from 1994 and took off at the end of the 20th century. Leading groups include the Aalto Acoustics Lab in Finland, the Institute of Technical Acoustics in Aachen, Germany, and the Technical Acoustics group (Technische Akustik) at TU Berlin. Auralization [4], published in 2007 by Professor Michael Vorländer of Aachen, can be seen as the founding text of this new branch of acoustics. Grounded in virtual reality, it covers the fundamentals, key techniques and applications of auralization in detail.

Today, auralization combined with VR is used mostly in the games industry, with Facebook Reality Labs (formerly Oculus) among the most successful. Elsewhere it hasn’t attracted much attention and remains largely at the level of concepts and research. Auralization itself still has many unsolved problems. To run in real time, for instance, propagation models still rely on simplified and not very accurate geometrical acoustics; reproduction can’t yet serve multiple listeners; and modeling of large and moving sources is still immature. I’ll cover auralization in detail in future articles, so I won’t go further here.

The marriage of acoustics with the latest technology, and the fresh perspectives and human-centered thinking it brings, have given architectural acoustics, the most traditional of acoustic disciplines, a new lease of life, full of potential business opportunities.
